doc.title: Catherine Russell interviewed by Monk Rowe, Utica, New York, October 26, 2018

title: Dancing with the Katherine Dunham Company and Aida at the Met
summary: She danced from age five, joined the Dunham Company at seven and performed Aida at the Metropolitan Opera, sitting at Leontyne Price's feet.

story.theme_name: First paying gigs: getting started as a young professional
story.community_name: First paid gigs: pay, bands and young beginnings

blocks.x: Yeah because they’d say, “Oh what do your parents do?” I said, “Well they’re musicians.” And people would say, “Oh, okay.” Because people didn’t think that was a real source of income. That wasn’t real work. So they went to work at night. They didn’t go to work in the daytime like everybody else. And so you know I didn’t really talk about Louis Armstrong for a long time, because people didn’t believe that my father — oh if you say, “Oh I was at Louis Armstrong’s house last night.” “Yeah, sure. Sure you were.” So yeah. So that’s kind of, you know and then my mother got me involved as a dancer first. So my mother got me involved in dance. And then I started working with the Katherine Dunham Company when I was seven, but I was dancing from when I was five years old. So I kind of grew up differently than, you know, my little friends.
And then you went to a drama academy, also?
That was much later. That was at the college level. I went to the American Academy of Dramatic Arts.
So the idea of being in front of an audience was, you got that at an early age and got fairly comfortable with it?

I would say pre-pubescent life I was very comfortable in front of an audience. I didn’t think about it. I just remember being at the Metropolitan Opera House because when we did “Aida,” which was what I did with the Katherine Dunham Dance Company, we did that for four seasons from 1963 to 1967. So we were at the old Metropolitan Opera House for two seasons. They tore that down, they built Lincoln Center then we moved in to the new Metropolitan Opera House for two seasons. So I think we were at the old Met. And it was me and another kid. So it was like six dancers. So we were the youngest ones, then there were middle dancers that might have been eleven or twelve years old. We were like seven, eight years old. And then there were the older ones. So there were six female dancers that would do a dance in part of the second act of “Aida.” So we were African, you know, it was an African dance troupe. And I just remember sitting there before the show started, and going, oh, it’s a full house — thinking to myself, there’s a lot of people here. So we were sitting at the Queen Amneris was the character, and it was Leontyne Price. So we were sitting at the feet of Leontyne Price. And she said, “Hello” you know, and she was all dressed up in her Egyptian, or whatever it was. And it didn’t bother me a bit. Later on though, when puberty hit, I thought oh I’m not pretty, I’m not this, I’m not that, so then I started to get very nervous.
The innocence of youth, right? Like you didn’t know that this should be nerve wracking.
Yeah. I just wasn’t into a comparison of me and other girls and anything like that. I just said wow, this is a really cool job. You know it’s a job. We were working.
